items.title: 8.3 The Binomial Theorem When the Index n is a Negative Integer or a Fraction

source_refs.note: Book p. 157-158: 8.3 Binomial Theorem when n is a negative integer or a fraction, binomial series (|x| < 1), Note box, Example 15, box of particular cases (i)-(vi) for n < 0

blocks.text:
When \(n\) is a negative integer or a fraction, then
\[(1 + x)^{n} = 1 + nx + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{2}\]
\[+ \dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^{3} + \dots\]
\[+ \dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}x^{r} + \dots\]
provided \(|x| < 1\).
The series of the type \(1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{2} + \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^{3} + \dots\) is called the binomial series.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What is new here?
1. The series never ends. For a positive integer \(n\) the factor \((n - n) = 0\) appears in the \((n+2)\)th coefficient and all later terms vanish, leaving \(n + 1\) terms. For \(n = -1\) or \(n = \frac{1}{2}\) no factor is ever zero, so there are infinitely many terms.
2. The condition \(|x| < 1\) is essential. Only then do the terms get smaller and smaller so that the sum settles to a fixed value. Example: \((1 + x)^{-1} = \frac{1}{1 + x}\). For \(x = 0.1\), \(1 - 0.1 + 0.01 - 0.001 + \dots \approx 0.909\), and \(\frac{1}{1.1} = 0.909\dots\). For \(x = 2\), the series \(1 - 2 + 4 - 8 + \dots\) never settles, although \(\frac{1}{3}\) exists.
3. The first term must be 1. The form is \((1 + x)^{n}\); an expression such as \((4 - 3x)^{1/2}\) is first written as \(4^{1/2}\left(1 - \frac{3x}{4}\right)^{1/2}\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text:
The proof of this theorem is beyond the scope of this book.
Symbols \(\binom{n}{0}, \binom{n}{1}, \binom{n}{2}\) etc are meaningless when \(n\) is a negative integer or a fraction.
The general term in the expansion is
\[T_{r+1} = \dfrac{n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}x^{r}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why are the symbols meaningless? \(\binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}\) uses \(n!\), and \((-3)!\) or \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)!\) is not defined in this course. The product form \(\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}\) (from 8.2.2) needs only multiplication, so it works for any \(n\). That is why the general term is written in this form.

blocks.title: Example 15
blocks.problem: Find the general term in the expansion of \((1 + x)^{-3}\) when \(|x| < 1\).
steps:
Given: \((1 + x)^{-3}\) with \(|x| < 1\), so \(n = -3\).
To find: \(T_{r+1}\), the general term.
Method: put \(n = -3\) in \(T_{r+1} = \frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}x^{r}\), take the minus signs out, and write the product with factorials so that it cancels.

Step 1: Substitute \(n = -3\)
\[T_{r+1} = \dfrac{(-3)(-4)(-5)\cdots(-3-r+1)}{r!}x^{r}\]
Why: the factors go down by 1 from \(n = -3\); the last one is \(n - r + 1 = -3 - r + 1 = -(r + 2)\). There are \(r\) factors.

Step 2: Take out the minus signs
\[= \dfrac{(-1)^{r}\cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5\cdots(r+2)}{r!}x^{r}\]
Why: each of the \(r\) factors is negative, so they give \((-1)^{r}\) times \(3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdots (r+2)\).

Step 3: Complete the factorial
\[= (-1)^{r}\dfrac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5\cdots(r+2)}{1 \cdot 2 \cdot r!}x^{r}\]
\[= (-1)^{r}\dfrac{r!\,(r+1)(r+2)}{2 \cdot r!}x^{r}\]
Why: multiplying top and bottom by \(1 \cdot 2\) turns the top into \((r+2)! = r!\,(r+1)(r+2)\).

Step 4: Cancel \(r!\)
\[T_{r+1} = (-1)^{r}\dfrac{(r+1)(r+2)}{2}x^{r}\]
Why: \(r!\) appears in the numerator and the denominator.

Check:
\(r = 0\): \(1\); \(r = 1\): \(-\frac{2 \cdot 3}{2}x = -3x\); \(r = 2\): \(\frac{3 \cdot 4}{2}x^{2} = 6x^{2}\); \(r = 3\): \(-10x^{3}\). So \((1 + x)^{-3} = 1 - 3x + 6x^{2} - 10x^{3} + \dots\), which agrees with the series given by computer algebra (and with case (iii) in the box below).

blocks.title: Some particular cases of the expansion of (1 + x)^n, n < 0
Teaching note
blocks.text: Cases (iv), (v), (vi) come from (i), (ii), (iii) by replacing \(x\) with \(-x\): all the signs become \(+\). Case (iv) is the infinite geometric series with common ratio \(x\), whose sum is \(\frac{1}{1 - x}\) (Unit 6). Learn these six; they are used again and again in 8.3.1 and in Exercise 8.3.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. For a negative or fractional \(n\): \((1 + x)^{n} = 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{2} + \dots\), an infinite series, valid only for \(|x| < 1\).
2. The first term inside the bracket must be 1.
3. General term: \(T_{r+1} = \frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!}x^{r}\); do not use \(\binom{n}{r}\) here.
4. \((1 + x)^{-3}\) has general term \((-1)^{r}\frac{(r+1)(r+2)}{2}x^{r}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Stopping the series after \(n + 1\) terms: for \(n = -2\) there are infinitely many terms, not "\(-1\)" terms.
2. Forgetting the condition \(|x| < 1\) (or \(|2x| < 1\), etc.).
3. Using \(\binom{-3}{r}\) with factorials: \((-3)!\) has no meaning.
4. Losing the minus signs: \(n(n-1)\) for \(n = -3\) is \((-3)(-4) = 12\), positive.
